newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank says "no consensus" on M2 zone.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank says "no consensus" on M2 zone.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank on Thursday denied a top policymaker's assertion that all government agencies had agreed to lower the official target zone for M2 growth to 8-13 percent from 9-14 percent.

"Officials of the Council for Economic Planning and Development have suggested lowering next year's targets for money supply growth but that proposal has not gone into further discussion," the central bank said in a statement.
"No consensus has been reached," it said.
"The bank is evaluating the money supply growth target zone for 1997 and no decision has been made. We will announce that at the year-end news conference," it said.
The bank has called a news conference for December 31.

Chi Schive, vice-chairman of the Council for Economic Planning and Development, the cabinet's main maker of economic policy, had told Reuters on Thursday that government-wide agreement had been reached to lower the target zone.
"All related officials have agreed to lower the M2 target zone to 8-13 percent," Schive said by telephone.
"It's only a matter of timing when it will be done. We'll leave this to the central bank to decide."
The wording of the central bank's subsequent statement suggested that Schive had overstepped his bounds.
"The bank is the agency responsible for setting up and executing our monetary policy," it said tersely.
The central bank lowered the M2 growth target to the current 9-14 percent from 10-15 percent in December 1995.
A downward adjustment would reflect persistent failure of the key indicator of Taiwan's broadest money supply measure to reach even the bottom of the target zone in 1996.
The latest monthly reporting of M2 growth was for October, when it came in at a year-on-year 8.45 percent. M2 growth was 8.69 percent in September and 8.44 in August.
Economists have said it was unlikely that M2 would come in above nine percent in the final two months of 1996 despite signs that a fourth-quarter economic recovery is under way.
Schive cautioned the adjustment should not be seen as trying to influence monetary policy at a time of loose liquidity.
"It's not related to policy tightening. It's simply reflecting reality," he said.

Schive said the adjustment reflected the actual conditions now seen in Taiwan's still-sluggish economy, which saw gross domestic product growth of 5.61 percent in the third quarter and is on track to reach only 5.7 percent for all of 1996.
"The money supply mainly reflects economic activity and expectations on inflation," Schive said. "If we expect low inflation, money supply growth should be conservative."
Taiwan inflation has remained under control at around three percent through 1996 and is on track to come in at 3.1 percent for all of 1996, according to government projections.

Inflation has remained low despite persistent looseness of liquidity in Taiwan's huge money market, where the central bank has pledged to maintain its "steady-to-loose" monetary policy to give any recovery the best chance of taking hold.
The central bank has vowed act to tighten money supply only if inflationary pressure rises or loose money is seen fuelling a stock market rally at the expense of currency stability.

Schive said global inflationary pressure was declining at a time of structural change in Taiwan's money market, where commercial paper and bond issuance is gaining popularity at the expense of bank lending and credit card use has soared.
"Direct financing is developing faster than indirect financing, and the use of plastic money has reduced actual money supply," Schive explained.

Central bank and other economic officials have expressed frustration that enterprises have not tapped the loose liquidity more aggressively, despite the attractiveness of rates at their current low levels.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong, explaining the bank's reluctance to tinker with interest rates, has said monetary policy adjustments were no "cure-all" for an ailing economy.
